power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Experiment-based calibration in psychology: foundational and data-generating model

author.affiliation:
Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Neuroscience
								Institute of Computer Science; and Medical Faculty
								University of Bonn
								Transdisciplinary Research Area "Life & Health"

text.text: Experiment-based calibration is a novel method for measurement validation, which -unlike classical validity metrics -does not require stable between-person variance.
In this approach, the latent variable to be measured is manipulated by an experiment, and its predicted scores -termed standard scores -are compared against the measured scores.

Previous work has shown that under plausible boundary conditions, the correlation between standard and measured scorestermed retrodictive validity -is informative about measurement accuracy, i.e. combined trueness and precision.
Here, I expand these findings in several directions.
First, I formalise the approach in a probability-theoretic framework with the concept of a standardised calibration space.
Second, I relate this framework to classical validity theory and show that the boundary conditions in fact apply to any form of criterion validity, including classical convergent validity.
Thus, I state precise and empirically quantifiable boundary conditions under which criterion validity metrics are informative on validity.
Third, I relate these boundary conditions to confounding variables, i.e. correlated latent variables.
I show that in the limit, calibration will converge on the latent variable that is most closely related to the standard.
Finally, I provide a framework for modelling the data-generating process with Markov kernels, and identify sufficient conditions under which the data generation model results in a calibration space.
In sum, this article provides a formal probability-theoretic framework for experiment-based calibration and facilitates modelling and empirical assessment of the data generating processes.
Experiment-based calibration is a technique for validation of measurement instruments.

The conceptual idea is to evaluate measurement accuracy by comparing the outcome of a measurement method or instrument against a standard, defined as the predicted outcome of a well-defined experiment.
This is a canonical technique in the physical sciences [14].
text.formatted: This is a canonical technique in the physical sciences <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: For example, the measurement of physical length can be evaluated against a standard based on the speed of light generated by a helium-neon laser.
Recently, a similar approach has been introduced to validate the the measurement of latent variables in experimental psychology, such as memory, attention, or perception [4, 3, 5].
text.formatted: Recently, a similar approach has been introduced to validate the the measurement of latent variables in experimental psychology, such as memory, attention, or perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: For example, the measurement of perceived lightness can be evaluated against standard values derived from physical luminance together with a formal theory of lightness perception (e.g., the CIECAM02 model).
Experiment-based calibration was introduced to physical quantities in the mid-20th century, long after the laws of physics were already well understood.
In consequence, there is little doubt in the physical sciences whether, and how, a calibration experiment generates the quantity that one would like to measure (i.e., the measurand ).
For example, there is no uncertainty that the helium-neon laser generates light that travels with an invariable speed, and the predicted outcome of an experiment can be very accurately computed.
In contrast, uncertainty about the effect of an experimental manipulation is likely higher in psychology and social sciences.
Sometimes, we can be quite sure that an experiment impacts on the measurand.

Physical luminance of an object influences perceived lightness, and the CIECAM02 model is a very good quantitative model of this impact-but even this model does not numerically capture all aspects, such as the Helmholtz-Kohlrausch effect [9].
text.formatted: Physical luminance of an object influences perceived lightness, and the CIECAM02 model is a very good quantitative model of this impact-but even this model does not numerically capture all aspects, such as the Helmholtz-Kohlrausch effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: In other instances, the relation might be even quite loose or speculative.

For example, when manipulating the number of practice trials in a learning task, this will on average affect resulting memory, but the numerical relation of trial number to memory cannot be precisely specified.
This raises two key questions. (1) If the relation between experimental manipulation and the latent variable is quite loose, can calibration still yield information on measurement accuracy?
text.formatted: This raises two key questions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> If the relation between experimental manipulation and the latent variable is quite loose, can calibration still yield information on measurement accuracy?

text.text: (2) If yes, and if several latent variables are loosely impacted by the experimental manipulation, then how can we be sure which one we are actually measuring?
For example, changing the luminance of an object changes its perceived lightness but might also affect its aesthetic perception, which we can think of as an "experimental confound".
How can we ensure, in a calibration experiment, that we are evaluating the measurement of lightness perception and not of aesthetic value?
To formalise such questions, we briefly recapitulate the calibration approach for psychological latent variables (figure 1) [3].
text.formatted: To formalise such questions, we briefly recapitulate the calibration approach for psychological latent variables (figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The standard value of a measurand is generated as intended or predicted value of a certain experimental manipulation; denote it with S. Denote the (unknown) true value of the measurand with T , and the measured value of the measurand with Y .
Because psychological variables have no natural scale, and actual scale might differ between samples and situations, comparing one measured value against one standard value bears little information.
Instead, we will realise several (two or more) values of S, and compare them with the ensuing values of Y .
Hence, S, T , and Y are defined as random variables, with the value of S randomly determined at every realisation of an experimental treatment.

This experiment will be done multiple times and with multiple persons (in a within-or between-subjects design), such that we can evaluate the correlation between S and Y, ρ SY , which we term retrodictive validity [2].
text.formatted: This experiment will be done multiple times and with multiple persons (in a within-or between-subjects design), such that we can evaluate the correlation between S and Y, ρ SY , which we term retrodictive validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: As will be shown in detail below, ρ SY depends, among other things, on the measurement error ε := Y -T .
Measurement error consists of two components.
The first is a random component, whereby Y takes different values on repeated measurements even when T is constant.
This corresponds to a lack of precision of the measurement [6].
text.formatted: This corresponds to a lack of precision of the measurement <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: The second component is systematic, whereby the average of Y , across repeated measurements of constant T , deviates from T .
This corresponds to a lack of trueness of the measurement (also termed bias) [6].
text.formatted: This corresponds to a lack of trueness of the measurement (also termed bias) <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Naturally, imprecision contributes to the variance of ε.
Perhaps counterintuitively, bias can also contribute to the variance of ε, when the bias is different for different values of T .
In contrast, a "global bias" (the average of Y deviates from the average of T ) is of no interest here because the anchor point of a psychological variable is usually unknown anyway.

Retrodictive validity, ρ SY , depends on error variance, so we can now compare two measurement methods by their retrodictive validity: the method with higher retrodictive validity will have lower error variance, which can mean higher trueness, or higher precision, or both.
Thus, retrodictive validity can be taken as a criterion to compare measurement methods.
This is conceptually similar to other forms of criterion validity [12], where the criterion is defined as the intended effects of the experimental manipulation.
text.formatted: This is conceptually similar to other forms of criterion validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, where the criterion is defined as the intended effects of the experimental manipulation.

text.text: To address the aforementioned key questions about uncertainty in the experimental manipulation, previous work has introduced the concept of experimental aberration ω := T -S, i.e., the difference between predicted and actually realised values of the latent variable [3].
text.formatted: To address the aforementioned key questions about uncertainty in the experimental manipulation, previous work has introduced the concept of experimental aberration ω := T -S, i.e., the difference between predicted and actually realised values of the latent variable <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: As shown in the next section, retrodictive validity depends not only on measurement error but also on experimental aberration.

In psychological experiments -in contrast to calibration in physicsexperimental aberration will presumably depend on the specific sample and experimental minutiae in ways that are often not understood in detail.
Thus, it might differ between two similar calibration experiments.
Hence, previous work has proposed to pitch two measurement methods against each other within the same experiment [3].
text.formatted: Hence, previous work has proposed to pitch two measurement methods against each other within the same experiment <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: In this case, experimental aberration is constant for all tested measurement methods.
This is particular simple when different measurement methods consist of different data transformations, applied to the same observables (e.g., reaction times).
However, there are also many applications in which different observables can be acquired simultaneously for comparison.
Examples are key presses for which response time and response force can be observed simultaneously [17], or the simultaneous recording of skin conductance and electrocardiogram [11].
text.formatted: Examples are key presses for which response time and response force can be observed simultaneously <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, or the simultaneous recording of skin conductance and electrocardiogram <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: While aberration is constant for all measurement methods calibrated simultaneously, retrodictive validity depends also on the covariance of aberration and measurement error, which is different between methods.
This is why previous work has analysed the covariance conditions under which retrodictive validity is informative on measurement error [3].
text.formatted: This is why previous work has analysed the covariance conditions under which retrodictive validity is informative on measurement error <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: In result, if measurement error is uncorrelated with experimental aberration, then a method with higher retrodictive validity is guaranteed to have smaller measurement error variance.
If this condition is not fulfilled, then there are boundary conditions under which ρ SY can be informative on measurement error.
These will be recapitulated below.
With the current article, I seek to fill, in probability-theoretic terms, four gaps left by previous work.
First, the previous model assumed a discrete distribution of S [3].
text.formatted: First, the previous model assumed a discrete distribution of S <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Here, I simplify and generalise the previous calibration model to arbitrary including continuous distributions of S and show that the previously derived boundary conditions remain applicable.

Secondly, I demonstrate that there is a dual problem in classical validity theory, where "construct-irrelevant variance" or "methods variance" is formally analogous to covariance between experimental aberration and measurement error in calibration.
I will show that the same boundary conditions apply to convergent validity.
Third, I address the problem of experimental confounds in calibration.
Finally, in order to enable simulations and theoretical work on the formal relationship between variables, I present a framework to model the data-generating relation between S, T , and Y.
This section simplifies the previous calibration model [3] and generalises it to continuous distributions of standard values S. With subscripted P, we denote probability measures.
text.formatted: This section simplifies the previous calibration model <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> and generalises it to continuous distributions of standard values S. With subscripted P, we denote probability measures.

text.text: We denote expectation and variance with E and V, respectively.
The model is illustrated in figure 1.

It is easy to see that a similar theorem holds for any calibration space.
In words, the theorem gives a boundary condition on Cor (ω, ε 1 ) and Cor (ω, ε 2 ) under which retrodictive validity is informative on measurement error variance.

Loosely speaking, if ω and ε are not "very" anti-correlated, then higher retrodictive validity can have two causes: either measurement error variance is lower (case 1) or the aberration-error correlation is lower (case 3), or both.
If, however, ω and ε are "very" anti-correlated, then higher retrodictive validity can also be caused by higher measurement variance (case 2).
In the next section, I show that this boundary condition is not specific to calibration and also applies to convergent validity, as often assessed in the context of classical validity arguments.
Assume we seek to measure a real-valued latent variable T with two different measurement procedures which result in measured scores Y 1 and Y 2 .
Then ρ Y1,Y2 := Cor (Y 1 , Y 2 ) is a convergent validity score.
Convergent validity assessment is performed to demonstrate that both methods measure the same latent variable and not two different latent variables that are only loosely correlated.

However, there is a possibility that the correlation between the two methods is high not because the methods converge on the same latent variable but simply because the measurement errors of the two methods are correlated [12].
text.formatted: However, there is a possibility that the correlation between the two methods is high not because the methods converge on the same latent variable but simply because the measurement errors of the two methods are correlated <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: A typical reason for such correlation is the presence of "methods effects", i.e. variance components that depend on the measurement methods, rather than on the true scores.
For a classical example from educational research, language abilities will affect any mathematics test that requires verbal reasoning.
Two mathematics tests that use verbal reasoning will thus be correlated, regardless of how well they measure mathematics abilities.
Such methods effects can be detected by assessing discriminant validity -i.e. the correlation between measured scores of two clearly different latent variables, established with the same method.

In our example, mathematics scores might correlate with scores on a history test which assesses a different latent variable, because the measurement errors are correlated, i.e. discriminant validity is low here.
Construct-irrelevant variance is perceived as a "threat to validity" [13], but how threatening is it really?
text.formatted: Construct-irrelevant variance is perceived as a "threat to validity" <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, but how threatening is it really?

text.text: In an application scenario, discriminant validity will often be non-zero because measurement instruments for the same latent variable typically target the same response channels (e.g., both requiring language).
However, the literature does not provide clear bounds on what values of discriminant validity are acceptable.
Within the calibration framework, we can derive these bounds:

Assume, without loss of applicability, that (Ω, A, P; Y 1 , T, Y 2 ) fulfills the formal definition of a standardised calibration space, where T is the latent variable that both measurement methods purport to measure.
Obviously, this calibration space is not orthogonal.
The measurement errors for the two methods are ε 1 := Y 1 -T , ε 2 := Y 2 -T .
Classically, one seeks to test whether both measurement methods tap into the same latent variable.
Equivalently, in our formulation we assume that they do measure the same latent variable T , and test the error in measuring this latent variable.

Theorem 6 gives the boundary conditions under which convergent validity is informative on measurement error.

In words, if the measurement errors are not "very" correlated then higher convergent validity means the methods have lower measurement error, but beyond this bound, convergent validity is strictly uninformative on the measurement accuracy, i.e. higher convergent validity then implies lower accuracy.
Deriving the exact bound requires knowledge of V (ε 1 ) and V (ε 2 ), which can be approximated from reliability assessment [12].

text.text: In this section, we dissect the reasons why a calibration space might not be orthogonal, i.e.
Cor (ω, ε) ̸ = 0.

At first glance, orthogonality appears very reasonable: experimental manipulation and measurement instrument are procedurally unrelated, unlike two different measurement methods in classical convergent validity assessment.

Hence, the measurement instrument does not "know" that on a particular experiment trial, the realised true score was higher than expected, and so cannot "counter" this with a particular value of measurement error.

The problematic case that Cor (ω, ε) < 0 (aberration and error are anticorrelated) would imply that (some of) the aberration, induced by the experiment, is subtracted from the true value during the measurement.
text.formatted: The problematic case that Cor (ω, ε) < 0 (aberration and error are anticorrelated) would imply that (some of) the aberration, induced by the experiment, is subtracted from the true value during the measurement.

text.text: Unless the measurement system is "informed" about the standard values or aberration, how could this possibly happen?
One explanation can be found in the notion of confounds.
Assume that many psychological latent variables are weakly correlated.
When we seek to manipulate or measure a psychological variable, then we might term any other latent variable that is correlated as confound.

Now assume that we seek to calibrate the measurement of a particular psychological variable T 1 , but both our experimental manipulation and the measurement system actually tap into a confounder variable T 2 .
To illustrate this with an extreme example, imagine that we seek to calibrate the measurement of aesthetic value.
However, our naive calibration experiment manipulates the luminance of of a physical stimulus, and our naive measurement instrument measures the perception of lightness.
Assuming that aesthetic value is weakly correlated with lightness, then the assumptions of a calibration space in definition 1 are fulfilled.
However, for each realisation of S, the true score for aesthetic value T will quite dramatically deviate from S.
In turn, because we are measuring lightness rather than aesthetic value, the measured value Y will again dramatically deviate from T , but in the opposite direction.
Thus, ω and ε are "very" anti-correlated.
From theorem 6, it follows that we can potentially increase retrodictive validity by increasing measurement error.
In doing so, Y will become an even worse measure of aesthetic value and, at the same time, become an even better measure of lightness, which however we are not interested in.
This demonstrates that non-orthogonality results from mis-specification of the latent variable T .
However, we can always find a more appropriate latent variable T ′ for which the calibration space is orthogonal (see lemma 4).
Non-orthogonality implies that for a given latent variable, both the calibration experiment and the measurement instrument are mis-specified in the same way.
We might sometimes have more subtle doubts about the appropriateness of the calibration procedure, and we might be wondering which latent variable we are actually measuring.
The crucial role of the calibration standard when arbitrating between confounds is discussed in the next section.

If both the experimental manipulation and the measurement method are much more closely related to the same confound then to the latent variable of interest, the the calibration space is non-orthogonal.
Now consider a perhaps more plausible case experimental manipulation and measurement instrument target different latent variables T 1 and T 2 .

For example, if we ask a person to state their level of confidence in a perceptual decision, then the experiment might directly manipulate the latent variable "confidence" (T 1 ), but the verbal expression (Y ) of confidence be mediated by a meta-cognitive representation of confidence (T 2 ), such that this meta-cognitive representation is more closely related to the verbal expression than the true confidence.
This can be modelled by assuming that T2 = T 1 + ω T where ω T is i.i.d. error.
To make the argument more general, we assume Cor (ω, ε 1 ) = Cor (ω, ε 2 ) = 0 and make no assumptions on the latent relation of T 1 and T 2 .
We want to know is whether a measured score Y is "more closely related" to T 1 or T 2.

text.text: In words, if the latent variable T 2 is "more closely related" than T 1 to the measure Y (i.e. has smaller measurement error), then T 2 will be "less closely related" to S (i.e. have larger aberration).
This reflects the previous intuition that the expression of latent variables in behaviour might be mediated by intervening variables.
In the example, the meta-cognitive representation of confidence T 2 will be less closely related than T 1 to any experimental manipulation that directly targets confidence ( T 1 ) as such.

In words, given a sequence of ever more perfect measurement methods, retrodictive validity is maximised by measured scores that are more closely related to T 1 rather than T 2 .

Thus, by maximising retrodictive validity, we converge on the latent variable that is more closely related to the standard S. In our example, this might correspond to an implicit measurement of confidence, which does not require a meta-cognitive representation.
This underlines the special importance of the calibration standard, and clarifies what we are measuring when nearperfect measurement instruments exist.

One might say that we have replaced the proverbial dictum "intelligence is what an IQ test measures" (definition of a latent variable by a measurement) with "intelligence is what a calibration experiment manipulates" (definition of a latent variable by an experimental manipulation).
This sits well with a contemporary approach of defining latent variables by substantive theory, rather than by measurement instruments [7].

text.text: The previous sections defined a calibration space as a tupel of a probability space and a set of real-valued random variables with minimal constraints, and analysed their interrelation.
Researchers will often be interested in modelling or simulating how these variables come about [1].
text.formatted: Researchers will often be interested in modelling or simulating how these variables come about <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: The goal of this section is to analyse how data-generating relations can be embedded in the calibration concept, and under which conditions they result in a standardised calibration space.
Throughout, we assume orthogonality, noting that we can always construct a non-orthogonal calibration space from an orthogonal one and vice versa.
This generative calibration model is based on two key ideas.
The first is to cast the data-generating relation as a three-stage probabilistic process with a starting distribution for S, and transition (Markov) kernels that specify T and Y .
This formalism provides a very general definition of a generative calibration space.
This definition is however rather abstract, and verifying whether any particular implementation fulfils the necessary conditions can be cumbersome.
To render the concept applicable in practice, the second key idea is to separate systematic bias from random imprecision [see 3, 1].
Thus, we specify deterministic non-linearities for systematic aberration and error, and conditional probability distributions for their random components.
This allows formulating a more intuitive and still quite general calibration model, together with sufficient conditions that are easy to verify.

To formalise the first idea, let the data-generating process start with standard values S. These are under the control of the experimenter, and hence the starting distribution P S can be freely chosen.
Once S = s is fixed in a realisation of the experiment, the experimental manipulation results in a true attribute value T = t, according to a probability kernel K S T (s, t).
The true kernel might depend on the experimental design in ways that are not fully knowable to the experimenter, but it can be modelled or simulated.
The experimenter then takes one or several observations, which are transformed into a measured score Y = y.
Given the fixed true score t, the measured score follows a kernel K T Y (t, y), which again is unknowable to the experimenter but can be modelled or simulated.
In this setup, Y is conditionally independent of S|T , which implies orthogonality,

Experiment-based calibration is a relatively novel approach to psychometrics in experimental fields [3], with several examples of practical application [2, 5] and simulations [1].
text.formatted: Experiment-based calibration is a relatively novel approach to psychometrics in experimental fields <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, with several examples of practical application <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref> and simulations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: The current work generalises and expands the previous work into several directions and thus contributes to laying a rigorous groundwork for this research program.
First, I show that previously derived boundaries under which retrodictive validity can be informative on measurement accuracy hold for any distribution of the experimental standard values.
Second, I show that the same boundaries apply in the assessment of convergent validity in classical psychometrics.
Third, I dissect the role of confounding variables, i.e.
variables that covary with the latent variable of interest.
When a single method is analysed, if this method relates more closely to latent variable T 1 than to latent variable T 2 , then T 1 will have a less close relationship to the standard values.
When multiple methods are compared under ideal conditions, then calibration will converge on the latent variable that has the closer relationship to the standard values.
This underlines the importance of the experimental standard.
Finally, I lay out a generative calibration model and derive identities that can be used for analytical and numerical modelling and simulations [1].
text.formatted: Finally, I lay out a generative calibration model and derive identities that can be used for analytical and numerical modelling and simulations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Experiment-based calibration requires that substantive theory allows predicting standard values in an experiment, and is thus suitable for consolidated research areas.

This reflects the approach of theory-based measurement, whereby any measurement of latent variables should be motivated and defined via substantive theory rather than by the measurement instrument (including its latent variable model) [7].
text.formatted: This reflects the approach of theory-based measurement, whereby any measurement of latent variables should be motivated and defined via substantive theory rather than by the measurement instrument (including its latent variable model) <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, calibration can also help solving a problem well-known in measurement theory: that there is an (unknown) non-linear mapping from the latent variable to the measured score.

Such non-linearity renders, for example, interpretation of non-crossover interaction effects in linear models ambiguous: what appears as an interaction at the level of the measured score might have been caused by a non-linear mapping from latent to measured score, when in fact there is no interaction at the level of the latent variable Loftus [10], Wagenmakers et al. [18].
text.formatted: Such non-linearity renders, for example, interpretation of non-crossover interaction effects in linear models ambiguous: what appears as an interaction at the level of the measured score might have been caused by a non-linear mapping from latent to measured score, when in fact there is no interaction at the level of the latent variable Loftus <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, Wagenmakers et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: While statistical techniques have been developed to identify such interactions Dunn and Anderson [8], calibration could aid solving the problem in a more fundamental manner.
text.formatted: While statistical techniques have been developed to identify such interactions Dunn and Anderson <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>, calibration could aid solving the problem in a more fundamental manner.

text.text: Non-linearities in the mapping from latent to measured score reduce trueness of the measurement -and thereby, retrodictive validity.
If this non-linearity were known, it could be embedded in the measurement model, thus rendering the mapping from latent to the resulting measured score linear.
This would, in turn, increase retrodictive validity.
In consequence, including various candidate non-linearities into the measurement model and selecting the one with highest retrodictive validity will, in the limit, minimise non-linearities.
As one result, this will improve the interpretation of interactions in substantive experiment using this measurement method.
As any tool, experiment-based calibration comes with limitations.
Most notable is the orthogonality assumption, i.e. that aberration and error are uncorrelated [3].
text.formatted: Most notable is the orthogonality assumption, i.e. that aberration and error are uncorrelated <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: In the present work, I show that violations of this assumptions correspond to a mis-specified substantive theory.
As another limitation, calibration does not cleanly separate trueness and precision.

Previous work has identified surrogate metrics that can be used for this purpose [3], and alternatively, calibration can be complemented with test-retest reliability assessment, which directly assesses precision [12].
text.formatted: Previous work has identified surrogate metrics that can be used for this purpose <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, and alternatively, calibration can be complemented with test-retest reliability assessment, which directly assesses precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Ultimately, it might be possible to derive clear metrics of uncertainty on psychological measurement [16, 15].
text.formatted: Ultimately, it might be possible to derive clear metrics of uncertainty on psychological measurement <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: With the present work, I hope to aid the modelling work that will put this approach into practice.
